clinicalPearls: Focal AT arises from a discrete atrial site and is driven by one of three mechanisms: abnormal automaticity, triggered activity, or microreentry within diseased atrial tissue; the term 'focal' distinguishes it from typical and atypical (macroreentrant) atrial flutter and does not by itself specify the underlying mechanism (p.1937).
It accounts for roughly 10% of paroxysmal SVTs in patients referred for catheter ablation, and may be sustained, nonsustained, paroxysmal, or incessant (p.1937).

Because focal AT is not dependent on AV nodal conduction, it does NOT terminate when AV block is induced and the atrial rate is unaffected by AV-nodal blockade — a key feature separating it from AV-nodal-dependent SVTs such as AVNRT and AVRT (p.1937).

P waves are typically discrete with an intervening isoelectric baseline (because atrial activation from a single focus occupies only a small part of the cycle), in contrast to the continuous undulating activation of atrial flutter / macroreentrant AT (p.1937).

A 'warm-up' phase (gradual acceleration of atrial rate after onset) or a 'cool-down' phase (gradual slowing before termination) favors focal AT with enhanced automaticity over AV-nodal-dependent SVT (p.1937).

Foci tend to cluster in areas of complex atrial anatomy — the crista terminalis, valve annuli, atrial septum, and atrial muscle sleeves extending into the thoracic veins (superior vena cava, coronary sinus, pulmonary veins) — and the focus location can often be approximated from P-wave morphology (p.1937).

P-wave localization clues: septal foci give a narrower P than sinus; left atrial foci give a monophasic positive P in V1 with negative P in I and aVL; superior foci (SVC, superior pulmonary veins) are positive in II, III, aVF; inferior foci (e.g., coronary sinus ostium) are negative in II, III, aVF (p.1937).

Atrial tachycardia WITH AV block is the characteristic arrhythmia of digitalis toxicity, so emergence of AT should prompt consideration of drug toxicity or another underlying illness; sympathetic stimulation promotes AT (p.1937).
Incessant focal AT can cause tachycardia-induced (tachycardia-mediated) cardiomyopathy, which is an important reversible cause of LV dysfunction (p.1937).
Asymptomatic nonsustained AT seen on monitoring is frequently mislabeled 'SVT' on monitor reports; treatment is NOT recommended for asymptomatic nonsustained AT identified on ECG monitoring (p.1937).
Frequent atrial ectopy and nonsustained AT are often precursors to more significant arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter (p.1937).

Vagal maneuvers, carotid sinus massage, Valsalva, or AV-nodal-blocking agents (e.g., adenosine) are used diagnostically to create transient AV block and unmask P waves when they are buried in the T wave or QRS (p.1937-1938).
harrison.pathophysiology: Focal AT originates from a single discrete atrial site and is caused by abnormal automaticity, triggered activity, or a small reentry circuit in diseased atrial tissue. It may occur in structurally normal hearts or in association with any condition causing atrial fibrosis, including atrial tissue scarred by prior catheter ablation. Zones of fibrosis serve as a nidus for abnormal automaticity arising from injured but partially viable cells, or for microreentry within and at the border of regions of slow conduction. Sympathetic stimulation is a facilitating factor, and the appearance of AT may signal underlying illness or drug toxicity (digitalis being characteristic). The arrhythmia activates the atria from a focal source through only a small portion of the cycle, producing discrete P waves with isoelectric intervals (p.1937).
additionalDifferentials: Sinus tachycardia (especially when the focus lies high on the crista terminalis near the sinus node, producing a near-sinus P-wave morphology; abrupt onset/offset favors AT)
AV reentry tachycardia using an accessory pathway (AVRT)
Atrial flutter / macroreentrant atrial tachycardia (continuous flutter waves, no isoelectric baseline)
Multifocal atrial tachycardia (multiple distinct P-wave morphologies)
nonInfectiousMimics: Atrial flutter and macroreentrant atrial tachycardia
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG to characterize P-wave morphology and the R-P / P-R relationship and to localize the focus
Ambulatory/Holter ECG monitoring (nonsustained AT is commonly detected and its prevalence rises with age)
Maneuvers to induce AV block (carotid sinus massage, Valsalva, adenosine) to expose buried P waves and to demonstrate that the atrial tachycardia persists despite AV block
Assessment for digitalis toxicity and other precipitating illness/drug toxicity when AT with AV block is seen
Echocardiography to evaluate for structural heart disease and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy
Electrophysiology study with electroanatomic mapping to identify the earliest activation (focal) site, typically prior to catheter ablation
redFlags: Incessant AT — risk of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy
AT with AV block — suggests digitalis toxicity or other underlying illness/drug toxicity
Rapid ventricular response causing angina, hypotension, pulmonary edema, or syncope
AT as a harbinger of atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter
harrison.prognosis: Symptoms vary widely and parallel those of other SVTs. Many nonsustained, asymptomatic episodes require no treatment. The principal adverse outcome is tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy from incessant AT, which is typically reversible once rhythm is controlled. Focal AT is frequently a precursor to atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter; however, the stroke risk and the indications for long-term anticoagulation are not considered equivalent to those of AF/flutter and remain unclear. Catheter ablation targeting the focus is successful in more than 80% of patients (p.1937-1938).
pitfalls: Mislabeling asymptomatic nonsustained AT on a monitor as actionable 'SVT' and over-treating it — treatment is not recommended in this setting (p.1937).
Confusing focal AT with sinus tachycardia when the focus is near the sinus node; rely on abrupt onset/offset and subtle P-wave morphology differences (p.1937).

Expecting AV-nodal blockade (adenosine, vagal maneuvers) to terminate the tachycardia — it usually only increases AV block while the atrial rhythm continues, since AT is independent of the AV node (p.1937-1938).
Overlooking digitalis toxicity or another precipitant when AT presents with AV block (p.1937).
Missing reversible tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy as the cause of new LV dysfunction in a patient with incessant AT (p.1937).
harrison.severityClassification: No formal grading scale; clinical stratification is by hemodynamic tolerance (stable vs unstable), by burden/pattern (nonsustained vs sustained, paroxysmal vs incessant), and by symptom status (asymptomatic vs symptomatic), since incessant disease carries the risk of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (p.1937).
management: Catheter ablation guided by electroanatomic mapping of the earliest activation site is the definitive, high-success treatment for recurrent or drug-refractory disease
Rate and rhythm control with beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, with antiarrhythmic agents such as flecainide, sotalol or amiodarone for suppression
Acute management with vagal manoeuvres and intravenous adenosine, recognising that the atrial rate may be unaffected by AV-nodal blockade
Identification and correction of precipitants, including withdrawal of digitalis and use of digoxin-specific antibody in toxicity, and correction of electrolyte disturbance
Recognition and reversal of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy through rhythm control, with echocardiographic surveillance of ventricular function
Observation with ambulatory monitoring and no treatment for asymptomatic, self-terminating nonsustained episodes
Cardiology and electrophysiology referral for mapping and ablation
